A.explanation: Resultant force is $-3.0\text{ N}$, so $F - 5.0 = -3.0$ gives $F = 2.0\text{ N}$.

B.explanation: This is the magnitude of the resultant force from $\Delta p/\Delta t$, not the applied force $F$ after allowing for the $5.0\text{ N}$ resistance.

C.explanation: This would balance the $5.0\text{ N}$ resistance to give zero resultant and constant momentum, but the graph shows momentum decreasing.

D.explanation: This adds the $3.0\text{ N}$ magnitude to $5.0\text{ N}$ instead of subtracting, which would give increasing momentum.

hints: Notice the momentum-time graph falls from $2.7\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to $1.5\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ in $0.40\text{ s}$, so momentum is decreasing.
Recall the gradient of a momentum-time graph equals the resultant force, $F_{net} = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Write the horizontal force balance with signs: $F - 5.0\text{ N} = F_{net}$ where $F_{net}$ is negative, then solve for $F$.
walkthrough: Read the graph values: initial momentum $p_i = 2.7\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0$ and final momentum $p_f = 1.5\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0.40\text{ s}$.
Calculate the change in momentum: $\Delta p = p_f - p_i = 1.5 - 2.7 = -1.2\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
Use impulse as rate of change of momentum to find the resultant force: $F_{net} = \Delta p / \Delta t = -1.2 / 0.40 = -3.0\text{ N}$.
The negative sign means the resultant acts opposite to movement. With $F$ forward and $5.0\text{ N}$ backward, $F_{net} = F - 5.0$.
Substitute: $F - 5.0 = -3.0$, so $F = 5.0 - 3.0 = 2.0\text{ N}$. This is option A.
